To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the proteolytic activation of influenza virus hemaggutinin is facilitated by different type II transmembran serine proteases.

TMPRSS2 and a newly discovered host protease, TMPSS4, both contribute to H3N2 viral activation and spread in vivo, and the combined deletion of these proteases strongly inhibits viral spread and protects mice against death after H3N3 influenza virus infections.
Tmprss4 is another host cell protease required for activation of H3 influenza viruses in vivo, and that Tmprss3 is not involved in activation of influenza virus hemaggutinin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of new host cell targets for treatment of H3N influenza virus infections in mice and humans.
identifying host factors that are essential for the activation and replication of different influenza viruses and thus represent potential targets for the development of new antiviral drugs.
the identification of host factors essential for the activation of influenza virus HA and thus represents a promising target for the development of new antiviral therapies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proteolytic activation of (H3) influenza virus hemaglutinin is facilitated by different type II transmembran serine proteases.
TMPRSS4 is not only a protease that is able to activate influenza virus HA, but it is also an important factor for the spread of H3N1 and H3N2 viruses in the respiratory tract of mice.
TMPRSS2 and, to a lesser extent, TMPRSS4 are involved in H3N2 viral activation in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

both Tmprss2- and Tmprss2/4-deficient mice are more resistant to H1N1 and H3N2 infection than wild-type mice, and that TMPRSS2 and 4 are the major host factors that facilitate H1N1 activation and spread, whereas TMPRSS2 is more important for H3N2 activation and spread than TMPRSS4.
Tmprss4 is a second HA-activating host cell protease for H3N2 viruses and that the combined deletion of Tmprss1, Tmprss3, and Tmprss5 is sufficient to block the activation of H3 viruses.
the HA cleavage activation of the H3N2 viruses is facilitated by two different type II transmembran serine proteases (TMPRSS2 and TMPRS44).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proteolytic activation of the influenza A virus hemagglutin is facilitated by different type II transmembran serine proteases.
targeting of host proteases for treatment of influenza infections is feasible and that the proteases TMPRSS2 and/or TMPRSS4 represent promising targets.
targeting of two host cell protease factors is more effective than targeting of only one factor.
